title: Spatial Heterogeneity in Angling Vulnerability Guides Management of Stream Salmonid Metapopulations
content:
ABSTRACT

Recreational angling often acts as a selective force, disproportionately removing large, highly fecund individuals, with potential consequences for population persistence. We investigated individual-based angling vulnerability in native white-spotted charr and red-spotted masu salmon in a dendritic stream network of tributaries and mainstem. Angling was size-selective, preferentially removing individuals with higher reproductive potential. Vulnerability was significantly higher in tributaries than the mainstem, likely driven by habitat and physiological condition. Population projection analysis indicated that angling throughout the system reduced the metapopulation growth rate below 1 in both species, with a pronounced decline in charr. However, closing either the tributaries or the mainstem to angling maintained their growth rates at sustainable levels. A portion of the system therefore needs closure, and we propose closing the narrow, small-area tributaries rather than the more extensive mainstem. This strategy maintains both conservation outcomes and recreational quality for highly sought-after native stream salmonids.
